questions.stem: A procurement specialist has spent most of a day in one very long chat negotiating terms on a supplier contract with Claude's help. A notice near the end indicated that Claude had summarized the earlier messages to free up space, and Claude's latest draft now paraphrases the liability cap loosely, giving the cap as 'roughly two million' instead of the exact figure agreed that morning. The final draft goes to legal tomorrow. What is the MOST reliable way to make sure the remaining drafting uses the exact agreed terms?

options.text: Ask Claude to re-read the whole summarized thread and reconfirm every figure it agreed on earlier in the same chat.
Switch to the most capable model in the same chat so that it can recall the morning's exact contract wording more accurately.
Start a new chat with the signed term sheet attached as the source of exact wording and a checked list of agreed terms.
Ask Claude to rate its confidence in each clause and flag any wording in the new draft that it feels unsure about.

questions.explanation: When a chat approaches its limit, Claude can **automatically summarize earlier messages** to keep the chat going — and those summaries are lossy: **exact figures and precise wording are the first things to blur** into approximations. A more capable model cannot recover detail that was compressed out of the conversation, and Claude's self-reported confidence is not a reliable accuracy signal. The dependable fix is to **re-anchor on the source of truth**: start a fresh chat with the document that holds the exact terms (the signed term sheet) plus a short, human-checked list of what was agreed, so Claude drafts from the precise text rather than from a compressed memory of the negotiation.

whyWrong.A: The earlier turns have already been summarized, so re-reading the thread tends to recycle the lossy summary rather than the original wording — and it keeps the work inside the same overloaded thread.
whyWrong.B: Switching model tiers cannot recover detail that was compressed out of the context. The problem is what is in context, not the model's capability.
whyWrong.D: Self-reported confidence is not a check against the agreed terms; Claude can be confidently wrong about a figure it only holds in summarized form.

questions.mindset: Summaries drop exact figures first; when precision matters, put the source document back in front of Claude.

questions.stem: A sales manager has a long chat in which Claude helped her analyze last quarter's pipeline, including several large spreadsheets. She now wants help writing a short, friendly welcome email for a new hire, which has nothing to do with the pipeline work. She has also noticed she is reaching her usage limit faster than usual this week. What should she do?

options.text: Start a fresh chat and give a short, complete request with the new hire's name, role and start date.
Keep working in the pipeline chat, since Claude already knows her preferences from that discussion so far.
Delete the spreadsheets from the earlier messages first, then ask for the welcome email in that same chat.
Upgrade to a plan with a larger context window so the pipeline chat can keep holding every unrelated request.

questions.explanation: Every new message is processed together with the whole conversation so far, so asking for an unrelated email inside a long, attachment-heavy chat spends usage on context the email does not need and invites the old topic to leak into the new one. A **new topic is the clearest cue to restart**: a fresh chat with a short, complete request is faster, cheaper and cleaner — which also eases her usage-limit pressure.

whyWrong.B: The pipeline chat's content is irrelevant to a welcome email; Claude does not need it to write a friendly note, and carrying it along costs usage while risking pipeline details leaking into the email.
whyWrong.C: There is no reliable way to strip attachments back out of past messages, and the thread would still be long and off-topic. A new chat solves it in one step.
whyWrong.D: Paying for a larger window to keep unrelated work in one thread treats the symptom; a bigger window does not make an off-topic history useful.

questions.mindset: New topic, new chat: don't pay for context the task doesn't need.

questions.stem: An events coordinator has a 120-message chat planning a three-city customer roadshow. Claude has started mixing up which venue belongs to which city, so he decides to ask Claude for a handoff summary and continue in a new chat. Which TWO actions will MOST improve the chance that the new chat continues the work correctly? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask for the handoff summary in as few words as possible so the new chat opens with a small, clean context window.
Ask the summary to list every confirmed decision with exact dates, venues and budgets per city, plus the rejected options.
Ask Claude to attach the full two-week transcript as an appendix to the summary so that no detail is lost.
Paste the summary into the new chat as-is, since Claude wrote it from the full history and it will be complete.
Read the summary through and check its venue-to-city pairings and figures against his booking records before reusing it.

questions.explanation: A handoff summary is only as good as what it captures and how carefully it is checked. Summaries are lossy for exact figures, names and pairings, so the summary should explicitly list **decisions, exact figures and names, rejected options (so they don't come back) and open questions**. And because the old chat was already confusing venues, the summary may carry the same error — he must **verify it against his own records** before using it. Otherwise the new chat starts with the mistake baked in.

whyWrong.A: Brevity is not the goal. A very short summary is likely to drop the exact venues, dates and budgets that matter most.
whyWrong.C: Attaching the whole transcript recreates the long, confusing context he is trying to leave behind.
whyWrong.D: The summary was produced by the same confused thread. Unchecked, it can pass the venue mix-up straight into the new chat.

questions.mindset: A good handoff captures decisions and exact facts, and a human checks it before it is reused.

questions.stem: A freelance consultant uses Claude with memory turned on. Next week she will run a live screen-share demo for a prospect and does not want Claude to bring up anything remembered about her other clients during the session. After the demo she wants everything Claude has remembered to work exactly as before. Which memory setting fits BEST?

options.text: Reset memory before the demo begins, then rebuild what Claude knows about her clients over the following weeks.
Pause memory for the duration of the demo, then unpause it afterwards so existing memories work again.
Ask Claude at the start of the demo to promise not to mention any of her other clients in its replies.
Delete each client-related topic from memory now, then re-enter those details by hand after the demo.

questions.explanation: **Pausing** memory stops Claude from using existing memories or forming new ones during the session, and the stored memories are kept — unpausing brings everything back exactly as it was. **Resetting** memory permanently deletes all of it and cannot be undone, which is the opposite of what she needs after the demo.

whyWrong.A: Reset permanently deletes all memories, including the client knowledge she wants to keep. She would lose exactly what she is trying to protect.
whyWrong.C: A verbal request is not a setting. It is less reliable than simply pausing memory for the session, and it leaves memories active in the background.
whyWrong.D: Deleting and re-entering topics by hand is slow and error-prone when a built-in pause does exactly this in one step.

questions.mindset: Pause keeps; reset erases. Pick the setting that matches what must survive.

questions.stem: An employee with memory turned on wants Claude's help preparing for a difficult personal conversation with his manager about a health issue. His company policy allows this kind of personal use. He does not want this topic to show up in future chats or be saved to his chat history. What should he do?

options.text: Use a regular chat, then tell Claude at the end that it should forget everything from this conversation.
Create a new Project for the topic so its separate memory keeps the topic away from his work chats.
Turn memory off permanently in the settings, even though he relies on it for his ongoing work tasks.
Run this one-off topic in an incognito chat, since incognito chats are not saved to history or memory.

questions.explanation: **Incognito chats** are built for sensitive one-offs: they are not saved to chat history and do not inform memory, so Claude will not reference them later. It is the smallest change that fully meets his need, and it leaves his work memory untouched. He should still follow his organization's data policy.

whyWrong.A: Asking Claude to 'forget' after the fact is not the same as never saving the chat. The conversation would still sit in his history and could be found later.
whyWrong.B: A Project's memory is separate, but its chats are still saved to history and the project's memory still records topics. It does not meet 'not saved'.
whyWrong.C: Overkill: turning memory off removes a feature he relies on for work — and it still would not keep this conversation out of his chat history.

questions.mindset: For a sensitive one-off, use the feature designed not to remember.

questions.stem: A marketing agency account lead handles two competing beverage brands. She has been doing both brands' campaign work in ordinary chats with memory turned on, and a colleague worries that Claude could carry one brand's positioning ideas into suggestions for the other. What is the MOST effective way to keep each client's context separate going forward?

options.text: Create one Project per client with its own files and instructions; each Project keeps its own separate memory.
Stay in ordinary chats but open every message by naming the brand and telling Claude to ignore the other one.
Reset all of her memory every Friday so that nothing from either brand's work carries into the next week.
Move to the most capable model tier, which is better at tracking which details belong to which client.

questions.explanation: Each Project keeps **its own memory, separate from other Projects and from ordinary chats**, along with its own files and instructions. One Project per client therefore separates the two brands' context by design rather than by remembering to say so in every message. She can also delete older cross-client topics in memory settings so nothing accumulated from the old ordinary chats keeps surfacing.

whyWrong.B: A prompt-only fix depends on her remembering every time, and it does not stop shared memory from accumulating across both brands' ordinary chats.
whyWrong.C: Weekly resets permanently delete useful memory and still allow mixing during the week — a blunt workaround for what a built-in feature does cleanly.
whyWrong.D: Model capability does not control what is stored in memory. The issue is where context lives, not how smart the model is.

questions.mindset: Separate clients, separate Projects: isolate context structurally, not by reminders.

questions.stem: A product owner on a Pro plan remembers that, about three weeks ago in a chat outside any Project, she and Claude worked out the reasoning for dropping a feature from the roadmap. A stakeholder now asks why it was dropped. She doesn't remember which chat it was and doesn't want to rebuild the argument from scratch. What is the MOST efficient approach?

options.text: Start a fresh chat, describe the feature from memory and ask Claude to rebuild the reasoning from scratch.
Turn memory on now and ask Claude what it remembers, since memory will fill in the details of past chats.
Ask Claude in a new chat to find the earlier conversation about dropping the feature and summarize its reasoning.
Scroll through her chat list one conversation at a time until she finds the right one, then copy out the reasoning.

questions.explanation: On paid plans, **chat search** lets her ask Claude about previous conversations in natural language; it searches her history and pulls in the relevant context. That recovers the original reasoning without repeating the work. She should still read the recovered reasoning before sending it to the stakeholder.

whyWrong.A: Rebuilding the argument may produce different reasoning from what was actually decided, and it wastes time and usage.
whyWrong.B: Enabling memory now does not create memories of past chats retroactively; memory only builds from conversations held while it is on. Searching past chats is the right tool.
whyWrong.D: This works but is slow. A built-in search does the same job faster.

questions.mindset: Before re-explaining, check whether a built-in feature can recall what you already did.

questions.stem: A compliance analyst must answer recurring questions about 40 internal policy documents over the next quarter. A colleague says: 'The newest models have huge context windows, so just paste all 40 documents into one chat and keep asking questions there; it will remember everything perfectly.' Which TWO actions reflect the BEST way to manage context for this work? Choose TWO.

options.text: Store the documents in a Project's knowledge so that any new chat can draw on them, with search across large sets.
Paste all 40 documents into a single chat as suggested, since a large enough window keeps accuracy from degrading.
Open a focused chat per question or topic and ask Claude to cite the policy section behind each answer.
Convert the 40 documents into a single merged file so that Claude reads them in order and remembers all of it.
Ask Claude to memorize the documents through its memory feature so that they no longer need to be uploaded.

questions.explanation: A larger context window does not mean perfect recall: as context grows, **accuracy and recall degrade ('context rot')**, so curating what is in context matters more than capacity. Keeping the 40 documents in a **Project's knowledge** makes them available to every chat in the Project, and large knowledge sets are searched for relevant content rather than loaded whole. **Focused chats per topic** keep each conversation short, and asking Claude to point to the policy section behind each answer makes the output easy to verify.

whyWrong.B: This is the exact misconception: a big window does not guarantee recall (context rot), and one endless chat also burns usage limits.
whyWrong.D: Merging the files does not change how much ends up in context; it is a manual workaround that ignores the built-in Project knowledge feature.
whyWrong.E: Memory stores useful topics from conversations; it is not a document store and does not replace uploading reference files.

questions.mindset: More context is not better context: persist sources in a Project and keep each chat focused.

questions.stem: A finance team lead keeps hitting her usage limit midweek. Her habit is to start each new chat by re-uploading the same budget workbook and policy PDF, then send many short follow-up messages one at a time ('now do Q2', 'now do Q3', 'now do Q4'). She wants to cut usage without losing quality. Which TWO changes will help MOST? Choose TWO.

options.text: Put the workbook and the policy PDF into a Project's knowledge once, so they're cached and cost less on reuse.
Switch every request to the most capable model so that each answer needs fewer follow-up corrections.
Keep everything in one continuous chat all week so that the files only need to be uploaded a single time.
Combine related requests into one complete message, for example asking for Q2, Q3 and Q4 all at once.
Turn off memory so that Claude stops storing topics and her remaining usage lasts noticeably longer.

questions.explanation: Two habits are draining her limit: reference files re-uploaded into every new chat, and many fragmented follow-ups that each re-process the growing history. Anthropic's usage guidance addresses both: keep reused files in **Project knowledge**, where content is cached and counts less against limits when reused, and **batch related requests into a single, complete message** (ask for Q2, Q3 and Q4 together) instead of many short follow-ups. Both cut usage with no loss of quality.

whyWrong.B: A more capable model consumes more of the limit per message and does nothing about the repeated uploads or fragmented requests.
whyWrong.C: One endless chat makes every new message carry the whole growing history, which uses more of the limit, not less.
whyWrong.E: Memory is not what is driving her usage. Turning it off removes a useful feature without addressing the real causes.

questions.mindset: Persist reused files in a Project and batch related asks; don't pay for the same context twice.

questions.stem: A recruiter is using Claude to rewrite a job description. Early on, Claude misread the role as fully remote, and although she has corrected it four times ('the role is hybrid, three days on site'), each new draft slips the remote wording back in somewhere. The chat is only about 25 messages long. What is the MOST effective next step?

options.text: Correct it a fifth time in the same chat, this time typing the instruction in capitals with far stronger emphasis.
Start a fresh chat with a complete prompt stating the hybrid, three-days-on-site rule up front, plus the current draft.
Ask Claude to explain why it keeps making the mistake before it attempts another draft of the description.
Switch to a larger-context model in the same chat so that it can keep all four corrections in view at once.

questions.explanation: The chat is short, so this is not a context-limit problem. The early mistaken drafts are still in the conversation and keep pulling later drafts back toward them. When Claude **repeats an error after several corrections**, the fastest fix is usually a clean restart: a new chat with a complete prompt that states the correct constraint up front (hybrid, three days on site) and includes the current draft, so the faulty drafts are out of context entirely.

whyWrong.A: More emphasis in the same thread leaves the faulty drafts in context. Four corrections have already failed; louder is not different.
whyWrong.C: An explanation does not remove the bad drafts from context and adds more back-and-forth before any fix.
whyWrong.D: The chat is nowhere near any limit. A bigger window does not remove the mistaken drafts that are causing the drift.

questions.mindset: When corrections stop sticking, restart clean; the bad history is part of the problem.

questions.stem: A customer service team member, working in a chat with memory turned on, accidentally pasted a customer's full account details into Claude while asking for help with a reply. Company policy says customer personal data must not be entered into AI tools and that incidents must be reported. He wants to handle this properly with the least disruption. What should he do?

options.text: Tell Claude to forget the customer's details and treat the matter as closed once Claude confirms that it will.
Say nothing about it, because the details were only used to draft a reply and nothing reached the customer.
Move the rest of the conversation to an incognito chat so the earlier pasted details are no longer saved.
Delete the chat, check memory settings for any saved topic about it, and report it under company policy.

questions.explanation: Telling Claude to 'forget' is not a data-protection control, and incognito cannot be applied retroactively to a chat that was already saved. He should **remove what he can** — delete the chat and check **memory settings** for any topic saved from it — and **report the incident under company policy**, which exists precisely for this situation. Context-management features help, but they do not replace governance.

whyWrong.A: A verbal promise from Claude is not a data control. The chat is still in history and the policy still requires a report.
whyWrong.B: Policy requires incidents to be reported regardless of whether harm is visible. Silence is a governance failure.
whyWrong.C: Incognito applies only to chats started as incognito. It does not retroactively remove details from the chat that was already saved.

questions.mindset: 'Forget this' isn't a control: remove what you can and follow the policy.

questions.stem: Five analysts on a Team plan each draft weekly vendor-risk notes. Each analyst keeps a personal 'rules' document (scoring scale, banned phrases, required sections) and pastes it into new chats, but the five copies have drifted apart and notes are now inconsistent. The team lead wants every analyst's chats to start from the same, current rules with minimal ongoing effort. What should she do?

options.text: Have each analyst turn on memory and tell Claude the rules once, so it remembers them in their future chats.
Email the current rules document to all five analysts each Monday and ask them to paste in the new version.
Set up one shared Project with the rules in its instructions and knowledge base, and give all five analysts access.
Have one analyst write all the notes in a single long chat so that the rules only need stating one time.

questions.explanation: The need is **shared, durable context** that stays consistent across people and chats. On Team and Enterprise plans, a **Project can be shared** with specific people, and its instructions and knowledge apply to every chat in it. One source of truth, updated in one place, replaces five drifting copies.

whyWrong.A: Memory is personal to each user rather than a shared, centrally updated source, so the five versions would still drift — and telling Claude the rules once does not guarantee they are followed weeks later.
whyWrong.B: This keeps the manual paste workaround that caused the drift; it relies on five people remembering every week.
whyWrong.D: It creates a single-person bottleneck and one huge, drifting chat. That is the opposite of good context management.

questions.mindset: Shared rules belong in a shared Project, not in five people's clipboards.

questions.stem: A research coordinator spent two weeks in one chat evaluating three survey platforms. Answers about one platform now include features that belong to another. She will continue the evaluation for another week, and the scoring criteria (security, cost, integrations, accessibility) must stay identical across all three. Which TWO changes would BEST address both the mixing and the need for consistent criteria? Choose TWO.

options.text: Keep the one chat but start every message with the platform's name in bold so Claude focuses on the right one.
Ask Claude to re-read the full two-week history before every answer so it can untangle which feature belongs to which platform.
Put the scoring criteria in the Project instructions so that every chat in that Project applies the same criteria.
Switch to a smaller, faster model so that answers are shorter and less likely to import other platforms' features.
Move each platform's evaluation into its own new chat, starting from a checked summary of that platform's findings.

questions.explanation: Two problems, two fixes. The mixing comes from three topics sharing one long context, so give each platform **its own fresh chat**, seeded with a summary she has checked herself. The consistency need is about **persisting** shared rules, so put the criteria in **Project instructions**, which apply to every chat in the Project. Together they separate what should be separate and keep constant what should be constant.

whyWrong.A: A prompt-only reminder leaves all three platforms in one crowded context, so the mixing can continue.
whyWrong.B: Re-reading the same tangled history does not separate the topics. It keeps the cause of the mixing in play.
whyWrong.D: A smaller model does not fix context mixing and may lower quality on a multi-factor comparison.

questions.mindset: Restart to separate topics; persist what must stay identical.

questions.stem: A communications manager is 18 messages into refining a CEO keynote with Claude. Each draft builds well on the last, Claude is following all of her tone and length notes, and the topic hasn't changed. A colleague recommends a team rule: 'Always start a new chat every 10 messages to avoid context problems.' What is the BEST response for this situation?

options.text: Stay in the current chat and restart only when there are signs like drift, ignored instructions or a topic change.
Follow the rule and restart now, pasting in only the latest draft so that the context window is cleared.
Restart now but paste in the entire conversation so far so that none of the accumulated tone and length notes are lost.
Turn on memory and restart, trusting memory to carry her detailed feedback into the new conversation.

questions.explanation: Restarting is a tool, not a ritual. Here the chat is working: one topic, instructions being followed, no drift. Restarting would throw away useful iterative context for no benefit. The right trigger for a restart is a **symptom** (drift, repeated errors, ignored rules, a topic change, usage pressure), not an arbitrary message count.

whyWrong.B: Pasting only the latest draft loses the tone and length guidance she gave along the way — exactly the context that is making the chat work.
whyWrong.C: Pasting the whole conversation recreates the same context in a new place, so there was no reason to restart at all.
whyWrong.D: Memory saves useful topics, not a full record of detailed draft feedback. Relying on it here risks losing her notes.

questions.mindset: Restart on symptoms, not on a schedule; healthy context is worth keeping.

questions.stem: A new hire at a company on a Claude Enterprise plan reads that memory can help Claude carry context across chats, but she can't find the memory option in her settings. She wants Claude to apply her standard report format in every chat starting this week, without breaking any company rules. What is the BEST course of action?

options.text: Use a personal Claude account with memory turned on for work reports until her company account matches it.
Put the report format into a Project's instructions now, and ask the admin whether memory can be enabled.
Paste a long 'remember this forever' message into her first chat each day so Claude keeps the format.
Report the missing option as a bug and hold off using Claude for reports until memory appears in settings.

questions.explanation: On Team and Enterprise plans, **memory availability is controlled by the organization's owner or admin**, so a missing memory option is expected behavior, not a bug. Project instructions persist her report format across every chat in the Project and are available today, while asking the admin about memory is the correct, policy-respecting route for that feature. She should not route work around her company's controls via a personal account.

whyWrong.A: Moving company work into a personal account sidesteps the organization's controls — a governance problem, not a workaround.
whyWrong.C: A message pasted into one chat does not persist to other chats, and with memory unavailable nothing is saved. She would be re-pasting daily.
whyWrong.D: It is not a bug, and halting report work is unnecessary when a built-in feature (Project instructions) meets the need immediately.

questions.mindset: Use the persistence feature you have, and ask the admin for the one you don't; never route around org controls.
